2nd Chance Survey: Descriptive Analysis

Sabina Rodriguez

05 November, 2026

Report purpose

This report presents the descriptive findings of the 2nd Chance Survey, examining the demographic characteristics, professional training, geographic distribution, and clinical practice settings of participating plastic and reconstructive surgeons in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA).

The analysis characterizes the surveyed workforce and identifies patterns in professional backgrounds, institutional affiliations, and geographic distribution that may inform further research and workforce planning.

Findings reflect the participating respondents and the facilities they reported and should not be interpreted as representative of the entire plastic surgery workforce in SSA.

Response rate and data completeness

Potential participants were identified through multiple sources, including the College of Surgeons of East, Central and Southern Africa (COSECSA), the 2nd Chance professional network, and publicly available online resources. The COSECSA membership lists identified 1,689 surgeons. The 2nd Chance network, developed through professional contacts and conference attendance, contributed an additional 64 surgeons not included in the COSECSA lists. Online searches of LinkedIn, search engines, and published literature identified another 32 surgeons not previously identified through either source. Together, these sources yielded 1,785 unique potential participants.

A total of 51 individuals accessed the survey. Of these, one declined informed consent, and eight were excluded because they were not currently practicing in Sub-Saharan Africa. Consequently, 42 participants met the eligibility criteria and were eligible for inclusion in the analysis.

During data cleaning, one respondent aged 50–59 years reported a specialty accreditation year of 1950, corresponding to 76 years since accreditation. As these values were inconsistent with the respondent’s reported age and could not be reliably corrected, both the accreditation year and derived years-in-practice variable were treated as missing for this observation. The respondent was retained in all other analyses for which valid data were available.

Respondent Characteristics

Age and Gender

The demographic composition of survey respondents was examined according to age group and gender. Together, these characteristics provide an overview of the age and gender representation within the participating surgical workforce.

Age Distribution

Respondents represented multiple age groups, indicating variation in career stages among participating surgeons. The age distribution is presented in Figure 1, highlighting the relative representation of surgeons across age categories.

Gender Distribution

The gender distribution of respondents is presented in Figure 2. Differences in the representation of gender categories within the sample provide context for examining the demographic composition of the participating workforce.

Age and Gender Distribution

The combined age and gender distribution is presented in Figure 3. This analysis examines how age groups are represented among male and female respondents, providing additional insight into the demographic composition of participating surgeons.

Country of practice

Survey respondents reported practicing across multiple countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, demonstrating the geographic reach of the participating workforce.

The geographic distribution of respondents is presented in Figure 4. The accompanying country-level comparison highlights the five countries contributing the largest numbers of reported surgeons.

Variation in participation across countries should be considered when interpreting the results, as the number of respondents may reflect differences in survey reach and participation rather than the underlying distribution of plastic surgeons across the region.

The combined figure places the five leading contributing countries alongside the regional map, allowing stakeholders to see both the broad footprint and the concentration of responses. Together, these visuals are helpful for discussing geographic coverage and possible gaps.

Professional Training

Professional training characteristics were examined to describe the educational qualifications, accreditation pathways, years since specialty accreditation, and current professional positions of participating surgeons.

Qualification

Respondents reported a range of professional qualifications, reflecting differences in educational and specialty training backgrounds. The distribution of qualifications is presented in Figure 5.

Accreditation

Survey respondents reported accreditation through different professional bodies. The distribution of accreditation bodies is presented in Figure 6, illustrating the diversity of specialty accreditation pathways represented within the sample.

Differences in national training and accreditation systems should be considered when comparing qualifications across countries.

Years Since Specialty Accreditation

The number of years since specialty accreditation was examined as an indicator of respondents’ professional experience following specialty qualification.

The distribution is presented in Figure 7, with the median indicating the midpoint of reported years since accreditation. Descriptive statistics, including the mean, standard deviation, median, and interquartile range, provide additional information about variation in experience.

This measure represents time since specialty accreditation and may not correspond directly to total years of clinical practice.

Subspecialty

Respondents reported practicing across several plastic and reconstructive surgery subspecialties, reflecting the range of clinical services represented within the surveyed workforce.

The distribution of subspecialties is presented in Figure 9. As respondents could select multiple subspecialties, the reported percentages represent the proportion of respondents identifying with each area of practice and are not expected to total 100%.

Practice Settings

Clinical practice settings were examined to characterize the institutions where respondents reported providing surgical services. The analysis considers facility characteristics, institutional ownership, geographic location, and the number of facilities associated with individual surgeons.

Because individual surgeons may practice at multiple institutions and multiple respondents may report the same facility, facility-level and respondent-level findings are presented separately.

Facilities Reported by Respondents

Survey respondents identified multiple healthcare facilities where they provided clinical services. The frequency with which each facility was reported is summarized in Table 4.

These results provide an overview of the institutions represented in the survey and the extent to which individual facilities were reported by multiple respondents.

Facility Distribution by level and Ownership

The distribution of facility ownership across healthcare facility levels is presented in Figure 10.

This analysis examines the composition of reported institutions according to their level within the healthcare system and ownership structure, allowing comparison of institutional categories within the surveyed facilities.

Urban vs. Rural Facility Distribution by Country

The distribution of reported facilities across urban and rural settings varied by country. Figure 11 presents the proportion of facilities classified as urban or rural within each country represented in the facility dataset.

These findings provide a descriptive overview of the geographic settings in which participating surgeons reported practicing.

Differences between countries should be interpreted in relation to the number of facilities reported and the coverage of the survey rather than as direct measures of national surgical service availability.

Multiple Facilities

Survey respondents reported different patterns of institutional affiliation, including practice at a single facility and practice across multiple facilities.

The proportion of respondents reporting employment or clinical activity at more than one facility is presented in Figure 12.

Number of Operating Facilities

The distribution of the number of facilities associated with individual respondents is presented in Figure 13.

These results describe the extent to which participating surgeons practice across multiple healthcare institutions and provide additional context for interpreting facility-level reporting within the survey.
